Title: Private credit's marks still owe reality a correction

Rating: underweight

Stonebeck Credit's gating of redemptions is not an isolated liquidity hiccup; it is the mechanism by which private credit reveals what its marks have been declining to say. The headline one_year_return of +6.0% sits awkwardly beside a ytd_return of -3.5%, and the reported_vs_public_gap of +1.0% is the footnote every allocator should read twice*: reported marks continue to run ahead of what public proxies imply, even as secondary bids are quoted in the low 80s. A discount of that magnitude does not appear in a healthy market; it appears in one where sellers know something the marking committee has not yet processed.

Consider the chart one would draw here: hy_spread_now_bps at 640bps plotted against policy_rate_now of 5.25% and cpi_now of 3.8%, with the private-credit NAV line laid across it almost flat, drawdown a modest -3.0%. The public line lurches downward with each redemption headline; the private line glides. Two markets, one credit cycle — the gap between the lines is not evidence of insulation, it is evidence of lag.

Calder & Root's view — that policy support resolves the stress — mistakes the absence of stated losses for the absence of losses. Policy rate stability does not repair impaired collateral or restore gated liquidity; it merely removes one variable from a still-fragile equation. Fragilities compound quietly in private structures precisely because marks lag reality, and gates are the first honest disclosure investors receive.

The risk to this view: if secondary bids in the low 80s reflect forced-seller distress rather than fundamental repricing, the eventual mark-to-market convergence could be shallower than implied here — a partial vindication of patience rather than a full unwind.

*A habit worth cultivating before the next NAV print.
